questions.text: A designer proposes a small bathroom space of 8 m² with 2.7 m ceiling height. The bathroom will use mechanical exhaust ventilation. What is the minimum required exhaust rate per PD 1096?

options.text: 50 m³/hour (based on 2 ACH)
216 m³/hour (based on 10 ACH)
272 m³/hour (based on 12.5 ACH)
No requirement; bathrooms do not need ventilation.

rationale.a: 2 ACH is insufficient for a bathroom; odors and moisture will not be adequately removed.
rationale.d: Bathrooms have specific ventilation requirements per code for health and comfort.
rationale.correct: Bathrooms and toilets require 10 ACH minimum per PD 1096 Section 809 for odor and moisture removal. Required exhaust = 8 m² × 2.7 m × 10 ACH = 216 m³/hour.
rationale.takeaway: Toilet/bathroom = 10 ACH. This is higher than offices (4–6 ACH) because odor and moisture must be removed quickly. Another high-risk category to memorize.

questions.text: What is the minimum required air change rate (ACH) for a hospital operating room per PD 1096?

options.text: 6 ACH, which is often considered insufficient for maintaining sterile conditions
10 ACH, a rate that may be suitable for other types of rooms but not for operating rooms
8 ACH, which is below the recommended standard for operating rooms

rationale.a: 6 ACH is appropriate for general hospital wards, not operating rooms.
rationale.b: 10 ACH is insufficient for OR requirements.
rationale.d: 8 ACH is lower than the operating room minimum.
rationale.correct: PD 1096 Section 809 specifies PD 1096 does not specify ACH by room type for ORs; use per-person rates per Section 811(b)(4). This high rate is necessary to remove surgical aerosols, blood particulates, and other biohazards. Additionally, operating rooms require positive pressure (room pressure slightly above hallway) to prevent infiltration of contaminated hallway air.
rationale.takeaway: Operating room = 15–20 ACH (highest standard). This is a critical distinction from regular hospitals (6 ACH). The higher rate and positive pressure control make OR the most stringent ventilation requirement in typical buildings.

questions.text: A classroom has a floor area of 250 m² and floor-to-ceiling height of 3.3 m. The design specification is 6 ACH. Calculate the required fresh air volume for this space.

options.text: 4,950 m³/hour
5,400 m³/hour
6,600 m³/hour
8,250 m³/hour

rationale.b: 5,400 m³/hour would be 250 × 3.3 × 6.5 ACH; slightly high but close.
rationale.c: 6,600 m³/hour would be 250 × 3.3 × 8 ACH; this would use the upper bound of classroom ACH (8), not the specified 6.
rationale.d: 8,250 m³/hour is excessive for a classroom.
rationale.correct: Fresh air volume = 250 m² × 3.3 m × 6 ACH = 4,950 m³/hour per PD 1096 Section 809 (classroom ventilation requirement is 5–8 ACH; this design uses 6 ACH, within range).
rationale.takeaway: This calculation reinforces the formula. Pay close attention to floor area, ceiling height, and the specific ACH (not a range, but the design value specified).

questions.text: A hospital operating room is 60 m² with 3.5 m ceiling height and a 18 ACH specification with positive pressure and HEPA filtration. An HVAC engineer proposes an air handling unit that supplies 3,500 m³/hour fresh air. Is this adequate?

options.text: Yes, 3,500 m³/hour exceeds the OR minimum.
No, the minimum requirement is 3,780 m³/hour (60 × 3.5 × 18).
No, OR requirements are 15 ACH, not 18; a lower capacity would suffice.
Yes, as long as the system includes HEPA filtration and positive pressure control.

rationale.a: 3,500 m³/hour is less than 3,780 m³/hour; it does not exceed the requirement.
rationale.c: The specification states 18 ACH, not 15. The design must meet the specified (or required) rate, not a lower minimum.
rationale.d: HEPA filtration and positive pressure are necessary but do not reduce the ACH requirement. All three factors (volume, filtration, pressure) must be satisfied simultaneously.
rationale.correct: Required OR volume = 60 m² × 3.5 m × 18 ACH = 3,780 m³/hour. The proposed 3,500 m³/hour is insufficient by 280 m³/hour. The shortfall may compromise surgical aerosol removal and positive pressure maintenance.
rationale.takeaway: Operating room is unforgiving. Every component—volume, filtration, pressure—must be correctly specified and maintained. An undersized fan (3,500 vs. 3,780 m³/hour) is a design error.

questions.text: A designer is evaluating two ventilation strategies for a small office (150 m², 3.0 m ceiling height): Strategy A uses mechanical ventilation with 5 ACH; Strategy B uses 100% natural ventilation (operable windows only). According to PD 1096, what is the primary design consideration for Strategy B?

options.text: Natural ventilation provides better air quality than mechanical; no concern, as it inherently meets all health standards
Natural ventilation must achieve 5 ACH through windows; the space must have operable window area ≥ 5% of floor area.
Natural ventilation is not permitted for offices; mechanical is mandatory due to strict air quality regulations
Natural ventilation requires no calculation; it depends on climate and window placement, which are assumed to be optimal

rationale.a: Natural ventilation quality depends on outdoor air quality and building design. In urban areas with high pollution, mechanical filtration may be superior.
rationale.c: Natural ventilation is permitted and preferred in low-rise buildings and tropical climates. It is energy-efficient and occupant-preferred.
rationale.d: While climate and placement matter greatly, the code specifies a minimum opening size (5% floor area). Design must meet this baseline.
rationale.correct: Strategy B requires operable window area ≥ 5% of floor area (1:20 ratio) per PD 1096 Section 809. For 150 m², this is 7.5 m² of operable windows minimum. Additionally, the design must ensure cross-ventilation or stack effect to achieve the desired ACH (in this case, approximately 4–5 ACH is typical for natural ventilation in tropical climates with wind). Natural ventilation is effective but less controllable than mechanical systems.
rationale.takeaway: Natural ventilation is a valid strategy but must satisfy the 1:20 operable window requirement. The effectiveness depends on building orientation, window placement (cross-ventilation), and outdoor wind patterns. For tropical Philippines, natural ventilation is often the preferred baseline with mechanical backup for peak loads.

questions.text: A hospital has a general ward space of 200 m² with 3.0 m ceiling height. A proposed mechanical ventilation system will supply 3,600 m³/hour of fresh air. Is this adequate per PD 1096?

options.text: Yes, 3,600 m³/hour exceeds the minimum for a hospital ward.
No, the minimum requirement is 3,600 m³/hour (exactly adequate, assuming 6 ACH).
No, the minimum requirement is higher (approximately 4,800 m³/hour for 8 ACH).
Yes, hospital wards have no specific ACH requirement if mechanical ventilation is used.

rationale.a: While technically adequate, the answer is misleading; 3,600 m³/hour exactly meets the requirement, not exceeds it.
rationale.c: 8 ACH would yield 4,800 m³/hour, but hospital wards are specified at 6 ACH, not 8 (which is classroom level).
rationale.d: Hospital wards have a specific requirement: 6 ACH per PD 1096, regardless of mechanical or natural ventilation.
rationale.correct: Hospital ward requirement = 6 ACH per PD 1096 Section 809. Required volume = 200 m² × 3.0 m × 6 ACH = 3,600 m³/hour. The proposed system supplies exactly 3,600 m³/hour, which is adequate (technically sufficient, though not exceeded).
rationale.takeaway: Hospital ward ≠ operating room. Ward = 6 ACH (routine patient care), OR = 15–20 ACH (sterile surgical environment). This distinction is frequently tested.

questions.text: A restaurant kitchen has a floor area of 120 m² and floor-to-ceiling height of 3.0 m. According to RA 9514, what is the minimum required fresh air volume for this space?

options.text: 1,800 m³/hour
3,600 m³/hour
5,400 m³/hour
7,200 m³/hour

rationale.a: 1,800 m³/hour would be 5 ACH—insufficient for a kitchen (needs 15 ACH).
rationale.b: 3,600 m³/hour would be 10 ACH—less than the 15 ACH kitchen requirement.
rationale.d: 7,200 m³/hour would be 20 ACH—excessive for a standard kitchen (20 ACH is reserved for operating rooms).
rationale.correct: Kitchen exhaust requirement = 10 ACH per PD 1096 Section 811(b)(2) for artificial ventilation. Fresh air volume = floor area × ceiling height × ACH = 120 m² × 3.0 m × 15 ACH = 5,400 m³/hour.
rationale.takeaway: The formula is: Volume (m³/hour) = Floor area (m²) × Ceiling height (m) × ACH. For kitchens, ACH = 15. Memorize this calculation pattern; it appears multiple times on the LEA.

questions.text: Compare three space types in a mixed-use building: (A) office 500 m² with 3.0 m height, (B) restaurant kitchen 100 m² with 3.5 m height, (C) hospital ward 300 m² with 3.2 m height. Rank these spaces by their required fresh air volume (from highest to lowest), assuming code minimum ACH for each.

options.text: Office (7,500 m³/hr) > Kitchen (5,250 m³/hr) > Hospital ward (5,760 m³/hr)
Kitchen (5,250 m³/hr) > Hospital ward (5,760 m³/hr) > Office (7,500 m³/hr)
Kitchen (5,250 m³/hr) = Hospital ward (5,760 m³/hr) < Office (7,500 m³/hr)
Office (7,500 m³/hr) > Hospital ward (5,760 m³/hr) > Kitchen (5,250 m³/hr)

rationale.a: The ranking is correct, but the office volume should be higher than hospital ward.
rationale.b: Kitchen should be lowest, not middle.
rationale.c: Kitchen and hospital ward are not equal; kitchen is lower volume.
rationale.d: Correct ranking and volumes. This demonstrates that total fresh air requirement depends on both ACH (space type hazard) and floor area (occupancy load).
rationale.correct: Calculations: Office = 500 × 3.0 × 5 ACH = 7,500 m³/hr (using 5 as mid-range of 4–6 ACH). Hospital ward = 300 × 3.2 × 6 ACH = 5,760 m³/hr. Kitchen = 100 × 3.5 × 15 ACH = 5,250 m³/hr. Ranking: 7,500 > 5,760 > 5,250. The office has the largest total volume despite lower ACH because it has the largest floor area. The kitchen has the highest ACH but smallest floor area, yielding the lowest total volume.
rationale.takeaway: This question tests synthesis: combining occupancy type (ACH) with geometric scale (floor area) to determine total ventilation load. Large low-ACH spaces can require more total air than small high-ACH spaces. Designers must consider both factors when sizing HVAC systems.

questions.text: According to PD 1096, what is the minimum natural ventilation opening requirement (in terms of floor area) for a space that relies on natural ventilation?

options.text: 2% of floor area, which is typically insufficient for spaces requiring significant air exchange
5% of floor area (1:20 ratio)
10% of floor area (1:10 ratio), ensuring adequate air flow and compliance with health standards
15% of floor area, often used in designs prioritizing maximum natural ventilation and energy efficiency

rationale.a: 2% is too low; insufficient for natural ventilation effectiveness.
rationale.c: 10% (1:10 ratio) is the requirement for daylighting, not ventilation. Note: these are separate metrics.
rationale.correct: PD 1096 Rule VIII Section 804(c) specifies a minimum of 1/20 of floor area must be operable window area for natural ventilation. This opening size provides sufficient fresh air exchange through natural stack effect and wind-driven ventilation.
rationale.takeaway: Remember: 1:10 for light (daylighting), 1:20 for ventilation (natural opening). These are distinct metrics and often appear together on the LEA.

questions.text: What is the minimum required air change rate (ACH) for a standard office space per PD 1096?

options.text: 2–3 ACH, which is typically used for residential spaces rather than office environments
3 ACH minimum
8–10 ACH, often applied in specialized industrial settings requiring higher ventilation
12–15 ACH, suitable for laboratory or cleanroom environments with stringent air quality needs

rationale.a: 2–3 ACH is too low for occupied spaces; CO₂ and odors accumulate.
rationale.c: 8–10 ACH is excessive for standard offices and increases energy consumption unnecessarily.
rationale.d: 12–15 ACH is reserved for high-risk or high-load spaces (kitchens, operating rooms).
rationale.correct: PD 1096 Section 811(b)(1) specifies minimum 3 ACH for office spaces. This range is sufficient to remove CO₂ buildup and typical indoor pollutants in occupied office environments.
rationale.takeaway: Office = 4–6 ACH. This is baseline. Any space with higher occupancy or contamination risk will have higher requirements.
